title: Naan-e sangak
subtitle: Persian pebble-baked sourdough flatbread
excerpt: Naan-e sangak is the most revered Persian bread: a long, dimpled flatbread traditionally baked on a bed of river pebbles in a wood-fired oven, giving it an irregular, craggy surface and a unique chewiness. This home version bakes on a very hot baking stone or tray to approximate the effect.
sourceNotes: Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Sangak documented as the highest-status Persian bread, associated with the military tradition of baking on heated stones. Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). The home version using a baking stone described.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked, cooled flatbreads. Reheat in a hot oven for five minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough rises slowly. Start three hours before you want to bake. Or make the dough the evening before and refrigerate overnight.
recipe.temperatureNote: The maximum temperature your oven can reach. Preheat for at least 30 minutes with a heavy baking tray or stone inside.

content.text: Naan-e sangak (sangak means small pebble in Persian) is a long, irregular flatbread traditionally baked on a bed of heated river stones that give it its dimpled, craggy surface. In a home oven, a preheated baking stone or heavy inverted baking tray approximates the intense, uneven bottom heat. The bread is slightly leavened, quite thin, and has a characteristic chewiness from the long prove. Topped with sesame and nigella seeds, it is the most celebrated Persian bread.
Make the dough and prove slowly

Mix {{yeast-dried}} and {{caster-sugar}} into 270 ml of warm water. Leave five minutes. Combine {{strong-bread-flour}} and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Add the yeast liquid and {{olive-oil}}. Mix and knead for ten minutes until the dough is smooth, soft, and slightly sticky. Oil the bowl, return the dough, cover, and leave for two hours until well risen.
At least 30 minutes before baking, place a heavy baking tray or baking stone in the oven and preheat to the maximum temperature, at least 250 degrees.

Divide the dough in two. On a sheet of baking paper, stretch each piece by hand into a long oval, about 40 cm long and 15 cm wide, 3 to 4 mm thick. Press your fingertips into the surface to make the characteristic dimples of sangak. The shape should be irregular, not perfectly uniform.
Scatter {{sesame-seeds}} and {{nigella-seeds}} over the surface and press lightly into the dough.

Slide the bread on its baking paper onto the hot tray or stone. Bake for six to eight minutes until the base is deeply golden and the surface has some golden spots and colour. The bread should be fully baked through. Eat hot.

items.symptom: The base is pale and not crispy
items.cause: Baking tray not preheated hot enough
items.fix: The tray must be smoking hot when the bread goes on. Preheat for a full 30 minutes at the maximum oven temperature.

items.symptom: The bread is stiff and crackerlike after cooling
items.cause: Baked for too long or rolled too thin
items.fix: Sangak should be no thinner than 3 mm. Remove it from the oven when golden: it will firm slightly as it cools.

items.cause: Dough springs back as it bakes
items.fix: Press the dimples quite deeply with your fingers, deeper than you think necessary. They will reduce by half in the oven.

items.symptom: The seeds fall off after baking
items.cause: Not pressed firmly enough into the dough
items.fix: After scattering the seeds, use the rolling pin or your palm to press them firmly into the surface.

content.text: Naan-e sangak is the most prestigious bread in Iran: more expensive, more work to make, and more loved than any other. The name refers to the small river pebbles that line the base of the traditional wood-fired sangak oven. The pebbles are heated to a high temperature and the dough is laid on them, giving the bread its irregular, textured surface and the smoky, caramelised spots on the underside. The bread has been recorded in Iran since the Safavid period (16th to 18th century) and was the bread of the army: soldiers carried the pebbles with them. A good sangak bakery will have a queue from early morning.
